lines.text: Hold up your thumb at arm's length, and look past it, at something far away.
Now close one eye… then the other. Your thumb jumps.
Nothing moved but your point of view. And that little jump, it turns out, can measure the distance to the stars.
For thousands of years, people looked up at those lights and wondered how far away they were.
But the stars never seemed to move. They looked pinned in place, like jewels in a cabinet.
Astronomers called them the fixed stars. And for two thousand years, nobody could say how far away a single one of them was.
The answer took a split telescope in Prussia, a woman with a magnifying glass, and one word scrawled on a glass plate.
And the answer turned out to be far stranger than the question.
A star is a dot of light. It has no size you can see, no edge, no label.
A bright star could be close… or huge, and very far away. From here, the two look exactly the same.
To find the distance, you need something you can measure. And the first clue was the one in your own eyes.
Clue one: the wobble.
Your eyes see from two places, a few centimetres apart. So a near thing seems to jump against a far one. That jump is called parallax.
Now spread your eyes as far apart as they could ever be: the two ends of the Earth's path around the Sun.
Look at a nearby star in January, and again in July. Against the stars far behind it, it should shift, very slightly.
Astronomers looked for that shift for centuries. So why did they see nothing?
The shift was there. But for every star, it is less than one three-thousand-six-hundredth of a degree.
In the 1830s, in Königsberg, Friedrich Bessel set out to catch it, with a telescope built for one job: measuring tiny angles.
His heliometer cut the image of the sky in two, so he could slide one star onto another and read the gap between them.
His target was a faint double star in the Swan, called 61 Cygni. It crawls across the sky faster than almost any other.
A fast crawl hinted that it was close. But how close? Night after night for more than a year, he measured it against two faint stars nearby.
In 1838 he had it: a shift of about a third of a second of arc.
That is the width of a small coin… seen from thirteen kilometres away.
From that tiny angle, the rest is a triangle. Its base is the Earth's orbit, and its far point is the star.
The answer: roughly ten light-years. About a hundred million million kilometres.
Its light had been travelling for about ten years to reach his telescope.
Bessel's number went into print, and for the first time, a star had a distance.
Almost at the same time, two more were measured: Alpha Centauri, from the Cape of Good Hope, and Vega, from Russia.
But there was a catch. Most stars are so far away that their wobble is far too small to measure.
Clue two: stars that blink.
Around 1900, Harvard College Observatory was photographing the sky on thousands of glass plates.
To study them, the observatory hired women, to measure and catalogue every star, one plate at a time.
One of them was Henrietta Swan Leavitt. Her task: find the stars that change in brightness.
Her plates came from a Harvard station in Arequipa, Peru, that photographed the southern sky, and two misty patches called the Magellanic Clouds.
Comparing plate after plate through her loupe, she found stars that swelled and faded, again and again… like slow breathing.
And she noticed something nobody expected: the brighter the star, the slower its breath.
All of them sat in the same cloud, at roughly the same distance. So the difference in brightness was real.
In 1912 she published twenty-five of them. The longer the period, the brighter the star: a straight line.
The circular was signed by the observatory's director, noting it had been prepared by Miss Leavitt.
Here was the trick. Time a star's beat, and you know how bright it truly is. See how faint it looks, and you know how far away.
Astronomers call such stars standard candles: like a candle of known brightness, carried further and further down a dark road.
Leavitt had found a measuring tape for the universe. She died in 1921, two years before it would change everything we knew about its size.
Clue three: one word on a glass plate.
Across the sky, astronomers had found faint spiral smudges. Were they clouds inside our own galaxy… or whole galaxies of their own?
In April 1920, at the Smithsonian in Washington, two astronomers argued it out in public. Neither could prove his case.
What they needed was a distance. And for that, you had to find one of Leavitt's breathing stars inside a spiral.
On Mount Wilson in California stood the largest telescope in the world, its mirror one hundred inches across.
Edwin Hubble turned it toward the great spiral in Andromeda, and photographed it on glass, night after night.
In October 1923, one plate showed a new point of light. He marked it with an N: a nova, a star that flares up once… and never again.
Then he checked the older plates of the same spot. It was not flaring once. It was brightening and fading, again and again.
He crossed out the N, and wrote three letters and an exclamation mark: VAR!
Variable. A breathing star. One of Leavitt's candles.
Its beat told him how bright it truly was. And its faintness told him how far: far, far outside our own galaxy.
Andromeda was not a cloud among our stars. It was a galaxy of its own. And it was not alone.
Clue four: galaxies that run.
Spread a galaxy's light into a rainbow, and dark lines appear in it. In most galaxies, those lines had shifted toward the red.
A red shift means the source is moving away, like the whistle of a train that drops as it leaves.
So why was nearly every galaxy running from us, and from each other? Picture raisins in a rising loaf.
In 1927, a Belgian priest and physicist, Georges Lemaître, had worked out what this meant: the universe is expanding.
In 1929, Hubble set his distances beside the speeds. The farther the galaxy, the faster it was moving away.
Think about what had happened.
People set out to measure how far away the stars are… and found that the universe is growing, and has a history.
Run the film backwards, and everything was once closer together, all the way back to a beginning.
And Bessel's trick never went away. A space telescope called Gaia has now measured the wobble of nearly one and a half billion stars.
Each one, a tiny tick of parallax: the same jump as your thumb.
So, how far away are the stars?
The nearest, a few light-years away: close enough for their wobble to give them away.
Farther ones, by the beat of their breathing stars. And the galaxies, farther than anyone had dared to imagine… and still drifting apart.
None of them ever left the Earth.
They measured the universe from a dome, a desk and a pile of glass plates.
And every distance out there still rests on that first small step: a wobble, seen from here.
So hold up your thumb tonight, and blink. That little jump is how we learned the size of the sky.
